Chapter 6





                                                                6-1

1. Discuss the important trends that have characterized
   labor markets in the U.S. and other countries
2. Apply a supply and demand model to understand
   the labor market
3. Explain how changes in the supply of and the
  demand for labor explain trends in real wages and
   employment since 1960
4. Define and calculate the unemployment rate and the
    participation rate
5.  Differentiate among the three types of
   unemployment defined by economists and the costs
   associated with each

• The rate of real wage growth has stagnated since
  1973
   – Fastest during the 1960s and early 1970s
• The number of people with jobs and the percent of
  the population employed has substantially increased
   – Driven largely by women entering workforce
• Data on real wage growth:
   – 1960 – 1973   2.5% per year
   – 1973 – 1995   -.75% per year
   – 1996 – 2010  1% per year
   – 1970 – 2012  0% per year

                                                                                                        6-4
                                                                        4

• Increased wage inequality in U.S
• Between 1960 and 2010
   – Average real weekly earnings of production workers
     decreased
          • Real wages of the least-skilled, least-educated workers
         decreased by 25 to 30%
   – Best-educated, highest-skilled workers' real wages
     increased
• Income with an advanced college degree is
   – Three times the income of a high school graduate
   – Four times the income of a worker who did not
     graduate from high school                                                                                                          6-5

• Produced by:
   – National Bureau of Statistics (国家统计局) in China
   – Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in the U.S. estimates
    employment and unemployment monthly based on
     surveys of about 60,000 randomly selected households
• Based on regular survey of households
• Based on “adult working-age” population
   – 15 to 60 years old in China
          • Compulsory education until age 15
   – 16 to 65 years old in US
          • Compulsory education until age 16

• Population divided into 3 groups:
  – employed: paid employees, self-employed,
    and unpaid workers in a family business
         • includes underemployed: work < 35 hours/week
  – unemployed: people not working who have
     looked for work during the previous 4 weeks
  – not in the labor force: everyone else
• The labor force is the total # of workers,
  including the employed and unemployed.
  – Working or looking for work

                                                                                                      6-14
                                                                          14

• Supply and demand analysis can be used to find
  the price of labor (real wages) and the quantity
  (employment)
   – Our analysis will consider the number of workers
     employed, not work-hours per year for convenience
• Labor market is an input market
   – Firms buy labor to produce goods and services
• Macroeconomics look at aggregate levels of
  employment and average real wages
   – Microeconomics looks at wage determination for a
     category of workers

                                                                                                     6-15
                                                                         15

• The demand for labor depends upon:
  – The productivity of workers
         • Greater productivity increases employment
  – The price of the worker’s output
         • A higher real price increases employment
• Diminishing returns to labor
  – Assumes non-labor inputs are held constant
  – Adding one worker increases output but by less
     than the previous worker added
• Value of Marginal Product (VMP) is extra
  revenue that an added worker generates

• Reservation wage is the lowest wage a
  worker would accept for a given job
  – Opportunity cost of working is your leisure
     activity
  – Work compensates you for lost leisure
         • If working conditions are unpleasant or dangerous,
       a premium for that would be included in the wage
  – Cost-Benefit Principle at work

• Macroeconomic determinants of labor supply:
  – Size of the working age population
         • Domestic birthrate
         • Immigration and emigration
         • Ages when people enter and retire from the workforce
  – Share of working-age population willing to work
         •  If supply is elastic, share of people willing to work
         increases as real wages increase
         •  If supply is inelastic, share of people willing to work is
         unaffected by changes in real wages

• A shift in labor supply is caused by any
  change in the number of workers willing to
  work at a given wage
  – Increase in the working-age population
         • Baby Boom
         • Higher net immigration
         • Increasing age at retirement
  – Increase in the share of working-age
     population willing to work
         • Women's participation in the labor force has
        increased in the last 50 years

• Stagnated growth in real wages could be caused by:
  – Slower growth in demand for labor, And/Or
  – Faster growth in the supply of labor
•  Productivity growth and real wages move together

• Slower demand growth due to slowed
  productivity growth explains slower wage
  growth
  – But does not explain rapid growth in employment
• Supply of labor must have increased as well
  – Increased participation by women
  – Baby Boom
  – High rates of immigration

  – Labor supply growth will slow
         • Baby boomers starts to retire
         • Women’s participation rate stabilizes
         • Falling birth rates, population growth slows
         • Immigrants get harder to find jobs
  – Partly depends on whether productivity
    growth continues to decline

• Globalization results in an expansion of many

• Benefit of globalization is increased specialization
  and efficiency
   – Principle of Comparative Advantage
• Globalization also means that some goods
  produced domestically are no longer competitive
   – Increased competition from foreign competitors
   – Some domestic sectors shrink and wages fall

• When wages in importing industries fall and wages
   in exporting industries rise, wage inequality
  increases
   – Low-skill industries face the toughest international
     competition
   – Political resistance to free trade grows
• Worker mobility is the movement of workers
  between jobs, firms, and industries
   – Market incentives move workers out of textiles and into
     software
   – Transition aid by government can assist workers to
    make the change
                                                                                                     6-41
                                                                         41

•  Technological change can be another source of increasing
  wage inequality
   – Occurs if technical change favors higher-skilled or
     better-educated workers
• Some innovation renders old skills less valuable
   – E.g. calculation skills of a clerk v.s. calculator and
     computer
•  Skill-biased technological change affects the marginal
  products of higher skilled workers differently from those of
   lower-skilled workers
   – Recent changes favor higher skilled workers
   – E.g. automobile production lines increasingly use robots

• Economic costs
  – Lost wages and production
  – Decreased taxes and increased benefit transfers
• Psychological costs
  – Lowered individual self-esteem
  – Family stress of decreased income and increased
     uncertainty
• Social costs
  – Potential increases in crimes and social problems
         • Social resources spent to address these

                                                                         49

• Costs of unemployment are directly related to the
  length of time a person has been unemployed
   – Unemployment spell is the period during which an
      individual is continuously unemployed
   – Duration of unemployment is the length of the
    unemployment spell
• The U.S. unemployed population in April 2011:

• Long-term unemployed have been out of work for
  6 months or longer
   – Permanently lowered life-time incomes
• Short-term unemployed have several possible
  outcomes
   – Find a permanent job after searching a few weeks
          • Economic costs are low
   – Discouraged worker, leave the labor force
   – Short-term or temporary jobs that leads to
    unemployment again
          • These chronically unemployed have costs similar to the long-
         term unemployed
   – Become long-term unemployed
                                                                                                     6-52
                                                                         52

• Discouraged workers would like to have a job but they
  have not looked for work in the past four weeks because
  they believe there are no jobs available
   – Counted as out of the labor force, not unemployed
   – Willing and ready to work
•  Involuntary part-time workers (underemployed) are
  people who like to work full-time but cannot find a full-
  time job
   – Counted as employed
•  U.S. August 2014 unemployment rate was 6.1%
   – Including discouraged workers and involuntary part-
     time workers would make the rate 12%

                                                                         54

■ Cyclical   ■ Frictional   ■ Structural
•  Cyclical unemployment is the increase in
  unemployment during economic slow-downs
   – Usually short term, associated with business cycles
   – Deviation of unemployment from ‘natural rate’
   – Can result in economic cost because of change in long-
      tern employment prospects of unemployed and lower real
    GDP growth
• The natural rate of unemployment
   – The normal rate of unemployment around which the actual
     unemployment rate fluctuates
   – Equal to Frictional + Structural unemployment                 6-55
                                                                         55

Even when the economy is doing well, there is
always some unemployment:
• Frictional unemployment occurs when workers
  are between jobs
   – Short duration for most workers, low economic cost
   – Workers spend time searching for suitable jobs
   – Can increase economic efficiency
• Job search is the process of matching workers
  with appropriate jobs
   – Workers have different tastes & skills, and
     jobs have different requirements
                                                                                                    6-56
                                                                         56

• Unemployment insurance (UI) is a government
  program that partially protects workers’ incomes
  when they become unemployed
• Increases frictional unemployment
   – Reduces incentive to find a job quickly
   – To work efficiently, unemployment benefits should be
          • For a limited time
          • Less than the income received when working
• Benefits of UI:
   – Reduces uncertainty over incomes
   – Gives the unemployed more time to search, resulting
      in better job matches and thus higher productivity

                                                                                                     6-57
                                                                         57

• Structural unemployment is long-term,
  chronic unemployment in a well-functioning
  economy
• Arises from some institutional structure in the
  society, economy or labor market
  – Lack of skills, language barriers, or discrimination
  – Structural shifts in production create a long-term
    mismatch between workers and market needs
  – Barriers to market equilibrium such as
         • Minimum wages
         • Unions
         • Government regulations, such as health and safety    6-58
                                                                         58

• Economic growth and technological change is
  associated with structural shifts in the economy
   – Innovation can cause older skills to lose value
      e.g. computers and skill with mechanical calculators
• Dislocated workers are workers who have
  become unemployed because of structural shifts
• Worker mobility is the movement of workers
  between jobs, firms and industries
   – Normal market incentives move workers from
      declining industries into growing industries.
   – Governments can aid transition by sponsoring job and
       skills training, adult and continuing education            6-59

•  Union: Worker association bargains with employers over wages,
   benefits, and working conditions
   – Typical union worker earns 20% higher wages
    similar to creating a minimum wage
•  Critics: Unions are cartels; they exert market power to raise
  wages above equilibrium, causing unemployment
   – “Insiders” – workers who are employed are better off
   – “Outsiders” – unemployed (not in the union) are hurt
•  Advocates: Unions counter the market power of large firms,
   leads to more efficient outcomes. Firms are more responsive to
   workers’ concerns
   – Promotes democracy in the workplace
   – Enforces workplace safety
